title: Campbeltown Whisky Explained | Craft Beer School
desc: What Campbeltown whisky is, why a small town became a protected Scotch region and the briny, oily style its malts are known for.
teaser: One small harbour town has its own Scotch region. Its malts taste of salt, oil and a little smoke.
standfirst: Campbeltown is a fishing town near the tip of the Kintyre peninsula with only a few working distilleries. It is still one of the five protected Scotch whisky regions. Here is why it matters and what to look for in the glass.
sections: A whole region in one town

Scotch whisky has five protected regions and Campbeltown is by far the smallest. It is a single town on the Kintyre peninsula in Argyll, on the west coast of Scotland, looking across the water towards Northern Ireland. Today it has three working malt distilleries.

That sounds odd until you know the history. In the nineteenth century Campbeltown had dozens of distilleries and was often called the whisky capital of the world. It had a natural harbour for shipping, local coal for firing the stills and good barley land nearby. The region status is a memory of that scale.
Why the town nearly lost its whisky

Most of those distilleries closed in the early twentieth century. The usual explanations are a fall in demand after the First World War, Prohibition in the United States cutting off an export market, the local coal running out and a reputation for some distillers cutting corners on quality during the boom years.

Whatever the balance of causes, the town went from dozens of stills to a couple within a generation. The survivors kept the region and its protected name alive. A third distillery reopened on an old site in the 2000s.
Salt, oil and a little smoke

The Campbeltown style is usually described as maritime, oily and robust. Typical notes are brine, sea spray, damp rope, toffee, dried fruit and a gentle wisp of peat smoke. Many bottlings sit between the light Lowland style and the heavily peated Islay style.

The oiliness is the part beer drinkers notice first. These malts coat the mouth more than a light Speyside does, closer to the weight of a strong Scotch ale than a pale lager. Our guide to mouthfeel in whisky explains where that weight comes from.

Be careful with the sea air story. Whether casks maturing by the sea pick up salt from the air is debated. A salty note can also come from the spirit itself or from peat cut near the coast. Taste the salt by all means. Just do not treat it as proof of where the cask sat.
Tradition shows up in the process

Campbeltown is known for keeping old methods alive. One of its distilleries still malts all of its own barley on traditional floor maltings, turning the germinating grain by hand. That is rare in Scotland today, where nearly all distilleries buy malt from specialist maltsters.

The same distillery is also known for running different distillation regimes for different spirits: double, triple and a partial method often described as two and a half times distilled. Distilling a portion of the spirit an extra time changes how much heavy, oily character survives. It is a useful reminder that a region's style comes from choices on the floor, not from geography alone.

A brewer will recognise the pattern. Two breweries in the same town can make very different lagers from similar malt, depending on how they mash, ferment and lager. In distilling the levers are the malt's peat level, the fermentation length, the shape of the stills, how fast they run and where the stillman makes the cut between heads, hearts and tails.
Peat level varies more than you expect

Campbeltown distilleries make a range of styles under one roof. A single distillery may produce a lightly peated spirit, a heavily peated one and an unpeated one, each sold under a different name. So the region on the label tells you less about smoke than it does on Islay.

Peat in malt is measured in parts per million (ppm) of phenols. Lightly peated malt is often in the low teens. Heavily peated Islay style malt is commonly 35 to 50 ppm or more. Read the bottle and the producer's notes to see which end you are buying. Our guide to peat and smoke in whisky explains the measurement.

Campbeltown malts are less common on Indian shelves than Speyside or Islay names. You will usually find them at specialist retailers, in duty free or in a friend's collection. Import duties vary by state. Because each bottle is a bit of an occasion, taste it properly.

Pour about 25 ml into a tulip glass. Nose it neat, then with a few drops of water. The oily texture often shows best neat. The coastal notes often lift with water. Sip slowly and look for how long the finish lasts. Drink water alongside and never drink and drive.

Picking brine from smoke or toffee from dried fruit takes practice. That gap between a vague impression and a precise note is what a trained palate closes.
Taste it next to its neighbours

Your first step: line up one Campbeltown malt between a Lowland malt and an Islay malt. Taste light to heavy. Note where the Campbeltown sits on body, smoke and salt. Three glasses side by side will teach you more about this little region than any map.
faqs: How many distilleries are in Campbeltown?
There are three working malt distilleries in Campbeltown today. In the nineteenth century there were dozens.
Some of it is. Campbeltown distilleries make lightly peated, heavily peated and unpeated spirits, so check the bottle.
What does Campbeltown whisky taste like?
Usually oily and full bodied with brine, toffee, dried fruit and a gentle smoke. It sits between the Lowland and Islay styles.
